summary: Describes what SCTP is good for, compares it with TCP and UDP, and gives guidelines on when to use it and when not to. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: SCTP is a reliable transport protocol like TCP, but it keeps messages apart instead of merging them into one byte stream, and it can fail over to a second network address without the application noticing. This memo compares it with TCP and UDP, lists the situations where it is the better choice, and covers what happens when it passes through a NAT.

subtitle: When SCTP is a better fit than TCP or UDP, and when it is not.

tldr.problem: TCP and UDP each fit some applications and not others, and SCTP was written to fit a third group, so implementers need to know when to pick it.
tldr.mechanism: The memo sets out the transport services each of TCP, SCTP and UDP provides, then lists the four things SCTP adds: multiple independent streams, multihoming with transparent failover, preservation of message boundaries, and unordered reliable delivery. It also covers SCTP's multihoming rules, its behaviour through a NAT, and the security differences.
tldr.outcome: The guidance is that most applications will find that either TCP or SCTP meets their needs, and SCTP is worth choosing when the extra features matter. The memo is Informational.

today: RFC 3257 is an Informational memo comparing SCTP with TCP and UDP, and the metadata does not list it as obsoleted or updated. It says the protocol had not been widely deployed at the time of writing, so further security issues might still be found and would need addressing in later revisions of the SCTP specification. It is read with RFC 2960, the SCTP specification itself.

sections.title: What the Memo Is For
sections.content:
SCTP is a reliable transport protocol which, along with TCP, RTP and UDP, provides transport-layer services for upper layer protocols and services. UDP, RTP, TCP and SCTP are currently the IETF standards-track transport-layer protocols. Each protocol has a domain of applicability and the services it provides, albeit with some overlaps.

By clarifying the situations where the functionality of these protocols is applicable, the memo says it can guide implementers and protocol designers in selecting which protocol to use. Special attention is given to the services SCTP provides that would make a decision to use SCTP the right one.

The terminology used in the memo is short. An association is the SCTP connection between two endpoints. A transport address is a combination of IP address and SCTP port number. The upper layer is the user of the SCTP protocol, which may be an adaptation layer, a session layer protocol, or the user application directly. Multihoming means assigning more than one IP network interface to a single endpoint.
sections.plainLanguage: Three transport protocols exist for the same job of moving data reliably, and each suits different applications. The memo's purpose is to make the choice easy by spelling out what each one promises the application above it.

sections.title: The Three Transport Service Models
sections.content:
TCP is a connection-oriented transport protocol. It requires the establishment of a connection before the exchange of application data and a tear-down to release system resources after the data transfer is complete. It is currently the most widely used connection-oriented transport protocol for the Internet. To the upper layer it provides data reliability, data sequence preservation, and flow and congestion control.

SCTP is also connection-oriented and provides all the transport services that TCP provides, so many Internet applications will find that either TCP or SCTP meets their transport requirements. For applications conscious about processing cost there might be a difference in the cost of running SCTP with only a single ordered stream and one address pair compared with running TCP.

UDP is connectionless, so applications that use it do not perform connection establishment or tear-down. As transport services to its upper layer it provides only best-effort data delivery and preservation of message boundaries. Applications that do not require a reliable transfer of more than a packet's worth of data will find UDP adequate, and some transaction-based applications fall into this category.
sections.plainLanguage: TCP gives a reliable, ordered stream and hides the connection from the application. SCTP gives the same reliability but keeps the messages separate. UDP gives no reliability at all and is used where a lost message can simply be sent again.

sections.title: What SCTP Adds to TCP
sections.content:
SCTP has some additional capabilities that TCP lacks, and these can make it a better choice for some applications and environments.

Multi-stream support: SCTP delivers multiple independent user message streams within a single association. Properly used, this alleviates the so-called head-of-line blocking problem caused by the strict sequence delivery constraint that TCP imposes on user data. It is particularly useful for applications that need to exchange multiple logically separate message streams between two endpoints.

Multi-homing support: SCTP provides transparent support for communication between two endpoints of which one or both is multi-homed. It monitors the reachability of the addresses on the remote endpoint and can fail over transparently from the primary address to an alternate address, without upper layer intervention. This can be used to build redundant paths between two SCTP endpoints, and is useful for applications that seek transport-level fault tolerance. Achieving path redundancy normally requires that both endpoints be equipped with multiple interfaces assigned with multiple addresses and that routing is configured appropriately.

Preservation of message boundaries: SCTP preserves application message boundaries, which is useful when the application data is not a continuous byte stream but comes in logical chunks that the receiver handles separately. TCP offers a reliable data stream with no indication of what an application may consider logical chunks.

Unordered reliable message delivery: SCTP supports the transport of user messages that have no application-specified order yet need guaranteed reliable delivery, which applications that prefer to use their own sequencing and ordering mechanisms may find useful.
sections.plainLanguage: Four differences matter. A stalled message no longer holds up the messages behind it. The connection can move to a second network address by itself when the first fails. The receiver gets messages as they were sent rather than as one merged stream. And messages can be delivered reliably in whatever order the application wants.

sections.title: Multihoming and NAT
sections.content:
Multihoming has the potential to provide additional robustness against network failures, which in some applications may be extremely important, for example in the signaling transport of telephone network signaling messages.

SCTP multihoming only deals with communication between two endpoints of which one or both is assigned with multiple IP addresses on possibly multiple network interfaces. It does not deal with clustered endpoints that can switch over to an alternate endpoint in case of failure of the original. For truly fault resilient communication the multihoming feature needs more than one IP network interface for each endpoint, and the number of paths used is the minimum of the number of network interfaces used by any of the endpoints. When an endpoint selects its source address, careful consideration must be taken: if the same source address is always used then the endpoint is subject to the same single point of failure. It should always select the source address to correspond to the IP address of the network interface where the packet will be emitted, subject to the binding address constraint, which is simply that the endpoint must never choose a source address that is not part of the association, so that the peer endpoint recognizes any source address used as being part of the association.

On NAT, when two endpoints are to set up an SCTP association and one or both of them is behind a NAT, the memo offers two options. When single-homed sessions are to be used, no transport addresses should be sent in the INIT or INIT ACK chunks. That forces the endpoint receiving the initiation to use the source address in the IP header as the only destination address for the association. The method can be used for a NAT, but any multi-homing configuration at the endpoint behind the NAT will not be visible to its peer, and so not be taken advantage of. For multihoming, the NAT must have a public IP address for each internal IP address it represents: the host can preconfigure an address that the NAT can substitute, or the NAT can have an internal application level gateway that intelligently translates the IP addresses in the INIT and INIT ACK chunks. If Network Address Port Translation is used with a multihomed SCTP endpoint, any port translation must be applied on a per-association basis so that the endpoint continues to receive the same port number for all messages within a given association.

The second alternative is to use the hostname feature and DNS to resolve the addresses. The hostname is included in the INIT of the association or in the INIT ACK, and must be resolved by DNS before the association is completely set up. There are special issues regarding NAT and DNS, for which the memo refers to the DNS extensions document for network address translators.
sections.plainLanguage: Behind a NAT, the simplest arrangement is to say nothing about your own addresses in the opening messages and let the translator's address be the only one the peer knows. Multihoming needs more: the translator needs a public address for each of your addresses, and any port rewriting has to stay the same for the whole association.

sections.title: Security Issues
sections.content:
Some TCP implementations have been known to be vulnerable to blind denial of service attacks, in which the attacker cannot see most of the traffic to or from the target host. The attacker sends a large number of connection establishment requests, that is TCP SYN packets, possibly from faked IP source addresses. The attacked host replies with SYN-ACK packets and enters the SYN-received state, allocating space for a transmission control block, and eventually the SYN queue fills up and the host has to start turning down new connection establishment requests.

TCP implementations with the SYN-cookies algorithm reduce the risk of such attacks. An implementation can switch to that algorithm when its SYN queues are filled up while still fully conforming to the TCP specification, but options such as a window scale cannot be used then. With the SYN-cookie mechanism a transmission control block is created only when the client sends back a valid ACK, so the three-way handshake has been successfully completed.

Blind connection forgery is another potential threat to TCP. By guessing valid sequence numbers an attacker would be able to forge a connection. However, with a secure hash algorithm, for some current SYN-cookie implementations the likelihood of achieving this is on the order of one in 2 to the power of 24, so the attacker would have to send that many packets before obtaining one forged connection.

SCTP was designed with the experiences made with TCP in mind. To make it hard for blind attackers to inject forged SCTP datagrams into existing associations, each side uses a 32 bit value called a Verification Tag to ensure that a datagram really belongs to the existing association: in addition to a combination of source and destination transport addresses that belong to an established association, a valid SCTP datagram must also carry the correct tag.

Unlike in TCP, the use of a cookie in association establishment is mandatory in SCTP. For the server, a new association is fully established after three messages containing INIT, INIT-ACK and COOKIE-ECHO chunks have been exchanged. The cookie is a variable length parameter containing all the relevant data to initialize the transmission control block on the server side, plus an HMAC used to secure it, computed over the cookie and a secret server-owned key. Additional resources for new associations may only be reserved when a valid COOKIE-ECHO chunk is received and the computed HMAC matches the one contained in the cookie. The chances of an attacker being able to blindly forge a connection are therefore even lower than with TCP using SYN-cookies, since the attacker would have to guess the HMAC value, lower than one in 2 to the power of 128.

SCTP only tries to increase the availability of a network. It contains no protocol mechanisms directly related to user message authentication, integrity or confidentiality; for those it depends on IPsec and on the security features of the application protocols. TLS using SCTP must always use in-order streams. At the time of writing the IPsec working group was investigating support for multi-homing, and to use IPsec one must use twice N times M security associations if one endpoint uses N addresses and the other M.

For both protocols, neither TCP nor SCTP protects itself from man-in-the-middle attacks where an established session might be hijacked. Both rely on a server-known secret key to protect the HMAC data, and the key must be created subject to the recommendations in the randomness document. The memo also notes that SCTP had not been widely deployed at the time of writing, so new security issues may yet be identified that would have to be addressed in further revisions of the SCTP specification.
sections.plainLanguage: Both protocols can be attacked by flooding the server with connection requests, and both use a secret key and a hash to make forged packets hard to produce. SCTP adds a 32 bit tag to every packet and makes the cookie step mandatory, which makes blind forgery far less likely. Neither protocol protects an established session against an attacker who can see the traffic, and neither provides encryption or message authentication on its own.

sections.title: The Functions SCTP Provides
sections.content: The memo's appendix lists the major functions SCTP provides: reliable data transfer; multiple streams to help avoid head-of-line blocking; ordered and unordered data delivery on a per-stream basis; bundling and fragmentation of user data; TCP friendly congestion and flow control; support for continuous monitoring of reachability; graceful termination of association; support of multi-homing for added reliability; some protection against blind denial-of-service attacks; and some protection against blind masquerade attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendix is the summary an implementer would keep: the full list of what the protocol does, from reliable transfer and multiple streams through to the built-in defences against blind attacks.

items.title: Multiple streams
items.text: Independent message streams inside one association, so a stalled one does not hold up the others.
